https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck79: The government has backed plans by former minister Alan Milburn for sweeping reforms to prevent "losing a generation" of young people to a life on benefits.
Milburn proposes spending billions on tailored support for under 25s not in employment, education or training (Neets), to be part-funded by cuts to some benefits.
He claims his plan, which also proposes tax breaks for firms and major education reforms, will get 440,000 young people into jobs by 2036.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he endorsed the "principles" of the Milburn review and was confident he could persuade Labour MPs to back legislation to implement its measures.

The PM told Sky News he would set out a full response to the review next month, after he had received a separate report into Personal Independence Payments (Pips) by Social Security Minister Sir Stephen Timms.
But he added: "I have never in my years in politics seen a wholesale, whole government approach to supporting the next generation.

"That is what this represents, and I am absolutely confident that I can take this vision and get people behind it, indeed get the country behind it, because we will not place Britain in the position I want it to be in if we have a generation of young people growing up without hope for the future."
The government has made Milburn the head of a new new youth opportunities unit to deliver on his recommendations.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said her party agreed with Milburn's "diagnosis" but claimed Labour had "made the problem much worse for young people" by increasing employers' National Insurance contributions and the youth minimum wage.
There are few signs so far that Burnham will face a backlash from his own MPs of the scale that blocked his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer's planned £5bn welfare cuts last year.
But some left-wing Labour MPs and the Unison trade union have warned proposals to cut health-related benefits will drive some young people into poverty.

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden told MPs that "in future" the welfare state should be judged "not just by a snapshot of people's monthly incomes" but "but by the story of people's lives, and by their ability to achieve their full potential".
McFadden, who was flanked by Burnham and Chancellor John Healey during his statement in the Commons, said the government rejected claims that young people were "snowflakes and shirkers".
The million who were not in work or training had been robbed of the "prospect of a good future" and that was something that demanded "much more" than a conventional government response, he told MPs.
He said the government would publish draft proposals on welfare reform early next year, with legislation to follow.
In his wide-ranging 250 page report , external , Milburn proposes:
An "entirely new benefits system" for under-25s, which would end the health-top up of Universal Credit and Personal Independence Payments (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales
Instead, a new "youth allowance" would be set at the basic rate of Universal Credit for under-25s, with a higher rate for those living independently
A reduction in employers' National Insurance costs for 21- to 24-year-olds, starting in the retail and hospitality sectors, meaning employing those young people would be cheaper
A huge expansion in post-18 college places and a legal right to work, education or training
A new, locally-led Youth Opportunity Service in England to give young people one named advisor and a personalised participation plan
Primary and secondary schools required to identify and support pupils at risk of becoming Neet, and schools obliged to offer work experience
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw8r: Review scores for GTA 6 are a fairytale ending after years of development
After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.
Does Grand Theft Auto 6, surely the most anticipated game of all time, live up to the hype?
Metacritic, which aggregates reviews from critics, averages it at 99 out of 100 , external - tying with Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which has held the record since 1998.
Reviewers overwhelmingly agreed the open-world action game was an ambitious, ground-breaking title that was well worth the wait.
Not everyone is enjoying the glowing praise - with some posters to online forums objecting to what one called "the ultra fan-boy hype."
But there is no question the reviewers have been effusive with their praise, with gaming website IGN , external branding GTA 6 "unprecedented", "unbelievable" and "unmissable".
Meanwhile in its five star review, Eurogamer said makers Rockstar had "pushed back the horizon of video games once again" with its graphics, storytelling and world building.
"The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome," reviewer Chris Tapsell wrote , external , but he added "there are also nits to pick".
For The New York Times , external one of those nits was whether the realism of the game might dull the fun chaos of its predecessors.
Reviewer Yussef Cole said GTA 6 had "matured beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups" with consequences to every action.
But "some of my favourite moments have been careening through streets with squad cars in hot pursuit," he wrote.
Critics say the relationship between Jason and Lucia is central to the game

The graphics of the game were hotly anticipated and so far have not disappointed critics, with The Guardian , external describing Leonida, the setting inspired by Miami, as "so lifelike that at times it beggars belief".
And the relationship between the lead characters, Jason and Lucia, has also stunned critics.
"They feel like real people rather than puppets dancing to your whim," The Guardian's Keza MacDonald wrote, adding: "I found it impossible not to care for them".
Writing for Forbes , external , Paul Tassi said: "I can't say I've ever seen a better video game relationship than the one they share".
The Washington Post , external said GTA 6 "raises the bar at every level", while Bloomberg , external 's Jason Schreier called it a "masterpiece" in his five star review.
"It's hard not to be astonished by what Rockstar has done here," he wrote. "There's nothing else like it.
"While playing this game, I often found myself wondering how it even exists."
Rockstar hasn't revealed the cost of the game, but some estimates put the figure north of $1bn (£760m).
Gaming journalist Jordan Middler is one of the lucky few in the UK who got early access from Rockstar and tells BBC Newsbeat it is the "game of a generation".
He'd played for about 100 hours by the time he hit the credits and says he still has so much to do.
Middler did spot one negative though - he found the game can "slow down" because of how much is going on.
He also says it is "long overdue" that there is a female lead in Lucia.
"The way previous GTA games have dealt with women has been a boys' club approach," he says.
"Introducing Lucia and not making her some kind of token character, she just fits in completely... and she will quickly become a fan favourite without question."
The Game Awards - the most watched ceremony of its kind in the industry - gave players a teaser of the critical reception when its 2026 nominations were revealed on Tuesday.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6z0: Outages and IT failings are commonplace - but not on this scale.

In the past week, there has been a massive Microsoft outage , an apparent tech glitch which grounded all US flights for hours , and issues for the National Security Agency (NSA). That's not to mention outages affecting the biggest US banks , as well as a major flaw found in a popular programming language .
These are all separate incidents - but the fact they have all come so close to each other has got people wondering if they might be linked.
There is no evidence to suggest this - but they do tell us a lot about how the modern tech world works, and where the vulnerabilities lie.
As is often the case, many outages were a result of an update or installation going wrong somewhere in a system.
A network upgrade at Microsoft caused servers to become overloaded and shut down.
It was also upgrades to a creaky old network which grounded thousands of planes in the US over the weekend.
Problems with the NSA's internal communication system and, separately, Apple's iCloud and Apple Pay were also blamed on things going wrong during system updates.
Disruption to payments in US banks has been put down to a "software bug" from JP Morgan Chase. The bank says it is not a cyber-security incident.
But some recent problems are in fact related to cyber-security vulnerabilities.
AI was used to discover flaws in Java, the third-most popular programming language in the world.
And researcher Scott Helme also discovered malicious code in Optimizely, a platform which is used by some of the world's largest companies.
Hackers were able to steal about $7,000 (£5,300) in cryptocurrency before they were discovered and kicked out.
Let's address the cyber incidents first - and the role of new AI models.
"I would be very surprised if all of these cyber-attacks and the attackers behind them were not using AI to accelerate themselves," Helme told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

Since the summer, AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI have decided it's too risky to give the general public access to the most advanced models before allowing certain companies and institutions to use them.
In these cases, security professionals can use the same tech to find flaws themselves and alert others before criminals get to them.
This happened in the recent Java incident , as well as the PHP one - where there was a scramble to patch the flaws before they could be exploited.
These are not new - the world stood still in recent years as CrowdStrike and then Amazon Web Services ground many devices and systems to a halt.
Part of this may be down to technical debt - a term used when operators go for quick fixes to software instead of solving an underlying problem.
A build-up of surface-level fixes can eventually end up with more serious problems down the line.
With AI causing many companies to re-evaluate their cyber-security, they may be issuing more updates to patch flaws they have found.
Outages are often also a reminder of the physical tech our online world relies on - such as cables, servers and data centres.
In the US air traffic control incident, for example, the problem came as engineers were replacing outdated copper wires with fibre.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is adamant the recent incidents are not connected or coming from one attacker.
"We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related."
In cases such as PHP and Java, the "good guys" found the flaws, with the help of AI, before the bad guys - allowing them to get together some fixes before the bugs could be widely exploited.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm87: A British hacker has been sentenced to six years in a federal prison in the US for conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies via text message phishing, and stealing more than $11.6m (£8.8m) in cryptocurrency from individual victims.

US prosecutors said the thefts had "severe, life-altering consequences" for victims and showed the growing threat posed by online crime groups.
The sentence brings to an end a years-long international investigation involving authorities in the UK, US, Spain and Canada.
Buchanan admitted taking part in a hacking campaign that began in 2021, when he was 19.
Working from his parents' home, he and other English-speaking hackers in the US and UK targeted employees at major technology and telecommunications companies.
It made them $8m in less than two years, according to US prosecutors.
Buchanan and his hacker gang sent out hundreds of SMS messages to the mobile phones of people who worked for large tech or telecoms companies.
The SMS phishing messages contained links to spoof websites designed to look like legitimate sites of victim companies.
The group used messages like "Hi, your account is due to expire - you need to log in to your work account here immediately or you will lose access to work apps".
The websites then lured the recipient into providing confidential information, including personal identifying information (PII), and account usernames and passwords.
The boys and young men did it on an industrial scale with Buchanan setting up a Telegram bot to collect all the victims' credentials as the duped workers unwittingly handed over their login details.

For some victim companies, subsequently stolen information included confidential work information, intellectual property, plus account access credentials, names, email addresses, and telephone numbers.
The group then used stolen information and SIM-swapping techniques to target cryptocurrency investors in the United States.
In the largest single theft, prosecutors said one victim lost $1.67m in December 2022.
Overall, authorities calculated that Buchanan and his co-conspirators stole more than $11.6m from victims.
In early 2023 his online identity and home address were leaked by rival hackers seeking access to his cryptocurrency.
Cyber security researchers and journalists reported that he was assaulted at his home and threatened with a blowtorch.

"TylerB and his group were highly sophisticated and organised but the violence he and others experienced was a sign of the troubling direction of these online communities of young hackers" says cyber security researcher Allison Nixon from Unit221B.
Buchanan then reportedly fled to Canada to escape further threats before returning home.
In April 2023, officers from Police Scotland searched Buchanan's bedroom after receiving a request from the FBI.
Investigators recovered a device containing the names and addresses of hacking victims, along with cryptocurrency seed phrases and account credentials belonging to at least one victim.
He was arrested on 31 May 2024 at Palma de Mallorca Airport in Spain while attempting to board a private flight to Naples.
After being extradited to the United States, he remained in custody before being sentenced this week.

In his November 2023 charge, Buchanan was named along with four American men and boys in their twenties and teens for alleged activity linked to the notorious cyber-criminal collective Scattered Spider.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cke8: A tech start-up used AI to uncover a critical software bug in Java that had existed for more than a decade (generic photo)
A cyber-security firm has used artificial intelligence (AI) to uncover a critical flaw in the hugely popular computer programming language Java.
Tech start-up Calif - which recently identified a cyber-security flaw in another language, PHP - found the bug in Java's memory functions.
Java is a popular programming language used by nearly all of the world's top companies such as Apple and Amazon, as well as many banks, hospitals and governments.
It is meant to make the IT world more secure by managing your memory online, said computer scientist Professor Toby Walsh, which is why "this is such an unlikely and serious flaw".
The discovery comes after a string of serious technology issues, including a massive Microsoft outage .
On Tuesday, the US National Security Agency said its internal communications went offline on Tuesday due to a "scheduled routine maintenance".
The NSA did not specify whether its outage was linked to the identified Java bug.
Apple also reported multiple services suffered full outages due to an internal update, while a network failure grounded all flights in the US.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was "zero evidence" the incidents were related .
With the help of AI, Calif discovered a serious security vulnerability it has called Java4Shell, which allowed an adversary to remotely execute unwanted commands to Java's memory system.
In this case, the adversary was OpenAI's recently-released model GPT-6 Cyber, which is not yet available to the public.
Oracle, the owner of Java, released a "critical patch update" on Tuesday, which it said contained security vulnerability fixes - including for this flaw.
At this stage it is unclear if any platforms or companies have been affected by the latest incident.
But the Java flaw remains a huge concern for cyber-security experts, who say overloading a system's memory is one of the most common ways for hackers to exploit or crash a system.
What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble?
US National Security Agency's classified internal network reportedly goes offline
Nearly every critical sector, including banking, national security systems, aviation and telecommunications, relies on Java.
First released in 1995, the programming language and computing system is now the "beating heart of the modern economy", Calif said in its investigation.
One of its main functions is to manage and protect memory for you, Walsh, a leading researcher in AI, told the BBC.
Any time you transfer information on the internet, receive a file from a user or need to log into an IT system with a password, the platform you are using is likely relying on a Java program.
The serious flaw could comprise "critical financial systems, customers and organisation's data," cyber-security expert Dr Pedram Hayati said.
In Australia alone, almost every bank uses Java for managing critical transaction data, Hayati added.
The latest incidents have exposed how nearly every critical sector - including national security systems, aviation and telecommunications - relies on legacy infrastructure online.
Earlier this week, thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, reported trouble accessing services.
The Java discovery follows a critical cyber-security flaw identified in the PHP programming language, also identified by Calif.
PHP is the code that websites like Wikipedia use to collect information and present it in a way you can read on the web.
Surrey Centre for Cyber Security Prof Alan Woodward said the PHP flaw affected some 30 million websites, leaving them vulnerable to malicious attacks.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art: Ten games into the Premier League season, four of the top six spots are occupied by 'big six' clubs.
Only second-placed Brighton , a club with a model which must be the envy of many of their rivals, and Premier League ever-presents Everton , have muscled their way in.
The six biggest clubs - Manchester United , Liverpool , Manchester City , Arsenal , Tottenham and Chelsea - now generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the division's other teams.
BBC Sport breaks down how the finances of the big six have exploded, examines new trends and the impact on the transfer market, and asks how much it really matters.
Companies put their money where supporters are prepared to spend it. It is a simple fact of business in every country, a reality of football's food chain.
In England, Liverpool , Arsenal and Manchester United traditionally dominated viewing figures, column inches, shirt sales and sponsorship.
Over the past 20 years they have been joined by Chelsea , Manchester City and Tottenham .
This group of clubs now generate so much money it is hard to imagine how they can fail in the long term - even factoring in short-term performance issues.
We will use Everton , the only club not in the big six to be in the Premier League since its inception in 1992.
This tells a tale of how even one of the league's founding members can be left trailing well behind.
In 2009-10, the gap in revenues between the big-six average and Everton was £120m. In 2024-25, that gap had grown to £442m.

Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool , told BBC Sport that it has attracted companies prepared to pay large sums to be associated with the Premier League's top clubs.
"The big football brand clubs have global fanbases and that makes them very attractive to global commercial partners, especially for sponsorship and front-of-shirt deals," Maguire said.

"You combine that with the fact that the Premier League is broadcast to 190 different countries around the world, and especially the international audiences - that allows the clubs to negotiate very good prices."
Only 10% of Everton 's revenue comes from commercial deals, while for the big six it is 45%.
It means Everton , and other clubs in the league, are heavily reliant on broadcast income. It makes up 66% of their revenue.
For Everton at least, this should change following the move to Hill Dickinson Stadium.
But that is unlikely to be enough to stop the gap increasing.
It has taken a few years, but Aston Villa and Newcastle have begun to increase their revenue.
This is largely thanks to the financial rewards of Champions League football.
But even Uefa has created a system which entrenches the position of the biggest clubs.
When the European Super League plan was torpedoed, Uefa created a new financial deal called the value pillar.
This reserves 35% of all Champions League revenues, or £713m, for the historically most successful clubs.
At the end of the league phase last season City are estimated to have earned £37.9m from the value pillar, Liverpool £35.5m and Chelsea £33.3m. Newcastle received only £13.6m.
The good news for Villa is their coefficient has improved greatly, aided by last season's Europa League win.
Their value pillar is projected to be worth £25m this season. But that will still be less than the big six clubs in the competition.
The cards are stacked against an ambitious club - not just domestically, but in Europe too.
Take a look at the financial trend of the big six and one thing becomes noticeable - Chelsea are beginning to fall behind.
In the past two seasons, and for the first time in recent history, the Blues recorded the lowest revenues of the big six.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/golf/article: LIV Golf - backed by more than $5bn (£3.8bn) from Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund - paid millions to players and executives in the weeks before filing for bankruptcy, while leaving a trail of unpaid bills from UK suppliers.
BBC Sport has seen invoices from five small businesses totalling hundreds of thousands of pounds, all of which were overdue before LIV made its final payments to players.
Global Infusion Group, , external a Buckinghamshire company that provided catering at July's LIV Golf UK event, is still owed £321,671, due on 7 August.
Suffolk-based BD365 Clean , external provided 108 cleaning staff and is owed £75,225, most of which was due on 20 July and 13 August.
"It just feels completely immoral," said Bonnie May, chief executive of Global Infusion Group.
"It really matters to a business of our scale. The impact has been huge, both personally and professionally."
Only $2m (£1.5m) has been earmarked so far by the Saudi owners to pay unsecured creditors, leaving many smaller companies unsure if they will receive anything at all.
Yet court filings reveal LIV made 59 payments to golfers on 31 July, amounting to $16.6m (£12.6m) and matching prize money for the same LIV Golf UK event.

A further $34.2m (£25.9m) went to players between 17 August and 3 September following tournaments in New York and Indianapolis, including $6.4m (£4.9m) to 2026 champion Jon Rahm just five days before the bankruptcy filing.
Four senior LIV executives also received retention bonuses totalling nearly $3m (£2.3m) in August.
"It's sickening," said Krissi Foskett, owner of BD365 Clean, who described the unpaid bills as "almost an extinction-level event" for her team.
"How can they sleep at night, knowing they are potentially putting companies out of business?"

Meanwhile, public records list more than £3,000 owed to Goodysphere, , external a family-run Yorkshire firm that provides a sensory bus designed to help autistic children who may find busy events overwhelming.
However, in August, LIV chief executive Scott O'Neil said he hoped they would be able to pay their suppliers.
"What I would say to them is we're doing everything we can to make sure we can do right by them and the work they committed."
Players received a total of $16.6m (£12.6m) five days after the LIV Golf UK event
The controversial breakaway league had been owned and bankrolled by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) since its launch season in 2022.
But in April, the fund announced it would end its backing after the 2026 season, putting LIV's future in doubt.
"Our understanding was that the funding would take LIV through 2026," said Global Infusion Group's May, whose company had about 60 staff catering for players and broadcasters.
"We weren't aware the funding had already stopped and there wasn't enough to actually fulfil their obligations."
PIF's multi-billion-dollar investment helped it to lure some of golf's biggest names and disrupt the PGA Tour's dominance of the sport.
"It's Saudi money, that's safe as houses, we thought," said Foskett.
"Their head honchos came along and enjoyed hospitality. We were there cleaning up at one o'clock in the morning then back in at five in the morning, only to be treated like this."
PIF remains the majority owner of Newcastle United, while Saudi Arabia will host the 2034 Fifa World Cup.

"I'm sure the country won't want to be saddled with the characterisation that it doesn't pay its bills," said professor Simon Chadwick, who is an expert in the business and politics of sport across Africa, Europe and Asia.
"I do find it surprising that they would simply walk away. I think they would want to engage in some kind of remedial action, particularly in terms of managing their image and reputation."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/darts/articl: Luke Littler's title defence is over despite an average of 101.38 against Jermaine Wattimena
Defending champion Luke Littler suffered a shock early exit at the Grand Slam of Darts after a stunning display from Jermaine Wattimena.
The Dutchman was in tears after securing a remarkable, and thoroughly deserved, 10-8 victory in the second round in Wolverhampton.

Having looked imperious as he won six legs on the spin to take a 7-2 lead, 16th seed Wattimena showed signs of nerves as the finish line approached, but dug in to stave off a late Littler comeback and progress to the quarter-finals.
"I think I played really incredible, I played my best game on this stage and I'm really proud of it," an emotional Wattimena told Sky Sports.
"He started playing well at the end. Last leg, [I had] one dart for the match - amazing."

Wattimena finished with an average of 101.70 having hit a staggering 10 180s and, such was his level for the majority of the match, he might feel the margin of victory should have been more comfortable.
The 38-year-old twice threatened nine-darters and had two darts for an 8-2 lead, with Littler rarely even given a look at a double.
However, the 19-year-old world champion sensed an opportunity and showed his class with a 10-darter to break throw as Wattimena finally stuttered a leg from victory.
But a dramatic comeback fell just short as, with Littler waiting to pounce on 65, Wattimena hit tops to take out 77 for the match and reach the last eight of the tournament for a second time.
Wattimena will face compatriot Kevin Doets in the next round after the world number 23 saw off Scotland's Cameron Menzies 10-5.
Doets averaged 101.51 and matched Wattimena's 10 maximums as his relentless scoring made up for an off night on the doubles.
Jermaine Wattimena will face fellow Dutchman Kevin Doets in the next round
Fourth seed Gerwyn Price is also through after a clinical display to beat Englishman Ryan Searle 10-7.
The Welshman averaged 103.31 and hit 45% of his doubles to see off 13th seed Searle, who himself averaged just under 100.
Price will face Niko Springer for a place in the semi-finals after he overcame former world champion Rob Cross 10-8.
Cross averaged 96.05 to Springer's 88.59, but the German's finishing was far superior - with a checkout rate of 48% - and that proved the difference.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/formula1/art: Lewis Hamilton is fourth in the 2026 F1 drivers' championship
Lewis Hamilton says there is "definitely not" a trust problem between him and his Ferrari team.
The seven-time champion has twice in the past four races ignored a call to pit for fresh tyres, both times to his competitive disadvantage.
The most recent time, in the Sao Paulo Grand Prix on 8 November, Hamilton stayed out on worn slick tyres in worsening rain and ended up spinning before pitting on the next lap.
Before this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, Hamilton spoke positively of his relationship with his race engineer Carlo Santi.
"We're constantly working on our communication," said Hamilton, who had a different race engineer last year.

"It's been a lot better this year. Carlos (sic) has done an amazing job. And those particular two times, particularly the last time, was just I didn't have the information I needed. I got the call right at the last minute.
"We'll just continue to work on the processes. We're super united in what's working, in the right direction."
The previous time Hamilton ignored a call to pit was in Singapore, when he decided to stay out during a virtual safety car period. He later apologised .

At the following race in Austin, he explained that he was "always looking at ways to win, always looking at doing potentially something different. And I wanted to be on a different strategy, not just the same strategy as Charles (Leclerc), where we just follow each other".
Ferrari's Hamilton-Leclerc problem - and other F1 stories to follow
'We've got big problems' - Hamilton says Ferrari need 'serious talks'

Hamilton and Leclerc both insisted that relations between the pair were good after clear-the-air talks in Brazil following a disagreement at the previous race in Mexico, where a tangle on the first lap led to them throwing away a potential one-two and handing victory to Red Bull's Max Verstappen.
Hamilton said in Las Vegas on Wednesday: "Charles is a great driver. The detail we went into about stuff like that in terms of when we close the visor, it's very clear we understand each other.
"We understand each other's boundaries and the ultimate goal, which is to get the best result for the team.
"So I don't feel that that will be a problem going forward. I have no concerns or worries about racing him, and I don't think he does with me either."
Leclerc said: "The discussion went very well. Very, very quickly, after a few sentences already, the tension that was there was not there anymore, and it was all fine.
"We both work in the direction of having that second place in the constructors' championship. The second place in the constructors' is important.

"It's also true that we've got a relatively big margin behind, which doesn't mean we need to minimise that, and we still have to work as a team. But what is really important for me now is to try and win before the end of the season and win the race."
He added that "everything has been taken out of proportion" but he is "kind of used to it" have been at Ferrari since 2019.
"Of course, the goal is not always to agree, and that will never happen," he added.
"We can have different opinions, and that was the case, for example, in Mexico. But just the fact of speaking eased all tensions, and we were completely fine with it.

"It's not that we had to speak for an hour, even though it ended up lasting an hour, just because we had a good time and we started speaking about also many other things in trying to bring the team and to help the team go forward.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/tennis/artic: Leandro Riedi reached the last 16 of the US Open men's singles in 2025
The clues were there. Leandro Riedi struggled to even force a smile after winning a match which moved him closer to the Wimbledon main draw.
These are the moments usually cherished and celebrated by a player ranked outside of the world's top 100.
The Swiss player's solemn reaction was jarring, but then nobody outside of his immediate circle knew what had happened a few days earlier.
Shortly before Wimbledon qualifying began in June 2024, Riedi had tried to take his own life.
Panic attacks had been plaguing the world number 137 for almost 18 months. Anxiety and self-doubt had been around for much longer.
The toll they were taking on his mental health meant he felt there was no other way out.
"I always had anxiety. I was always a shy person, especially when I was younger. I always had this mindset that I wasn't good enough," Riedi told BBC Sport.
"I always thought I needed to do something special. I have to be perfect. This was my mental battle all the time.
"February 2023 to November 2024 was a horrible period of time. I was always scared of having a panic attack. I had no control over it whatsoever."
Very few people knew the extent of Riedi's mental health issues until he revealed last week that he had attempted suicide.
Firstly, he is not looking for sympathy. He has only decided to talk about his experience to "send a strong message" for others struggling with their mental health.
Secondly, he is now in a "very good" place, thanks to professional treatment he has received over the past two years.
"I hope nobody ever has to go through what I did - it's horrifying and scary," Riedi said.
In his darkest moments Riedi found salvation in the sport which he started playing as a three-year-old growing up in Zurich.

He credits his psychologist, who stayed awake with Riedi until 3am to make sure he was not alone, for saving his life.

The catalyst of change came a few weeks later when a knee injury - the first "big injury" of his career - required surgery following the US Open.

There is no one-size fits all when it comes to determining great strikers, but they do all share a common trait - a ruthlessness in front of goal.
This week, however, we put the power in your hands to decide the best European frontmen of the 21st century.
Tens of thousands of you voted on the 20-man shortlist drawn up by our panel.
We then asked European football experts Guillem Balague, Julien Laurens and Raphael Honigstein to discuss your choices on the Euro Leagues podcast.
So from 10-1, here are the best European strikers this century - as voted for by you.

Karim Benzema comes in at number 10, the former Lyon and Real Madrid frontman's closest challengers coming from across the continent in the shape of Raul, Robin van Persie, Michael Owen and Miroslav Klose.

Laurens: "From a young age you could see he was something special. I know it was difficult at the beginning at Real Madrid, but in the post-Cristiano era he carried that team, wore the armband and won big titles and trophies by being decisive in big moments. Like I used to say 'Karim the dream'."

Honigstein: "The selflessness, the ability to work for the team. A sense of elegance and humility on the pitch, which is unusual in a goalscorer. I think he is unusual in that list. I think not many will define themselves through their teamwork and assists as much as their goals, but he was that player."

Ruud van Nistelrooy edges Benzema, with whom he briefly overlapped at Real Madrid - the Dutchman teed up the Frenchman and scored himself in their only La Liga appearance together, before he left for Hamburg in January 2010 following injury problems.
The former PSV striker's most consistent spell, of course, came at Manchester United, where he scored 150 goals.

Honigstein: "He is the nicest guy but he never came across that way on the pitch. Typical trait of a striker, he would kill to score the goal. I think anyone who has grown up with him scoring goals, for United especially, must have a soft spot for him because he was a phenomenal poacher."
Laurens: "He was a strong player physically, and despite the lack of pace the awareness in the box was just very special even with all the injuries."

Zlatan Ibrahimovic slots in at eight, comfortably clear of Van Nistelrooy and Benzema. The Swede netted more than 500 times in a career that spanned Malmo, Ajax, Juventus, both Milans, Barcelona, Paris St-Germain, Manchester United and LA Galaxy.

Balague: "He was a big-game player and that explains the league titles with PSG. Scoring four goals against England, the overhead kick. The personality thing has put him one or two places in this list, saying 'I am great, I am the best'. If you keep saying you're great it makes people stop and think."

Laurens: "The mentality of really believing he was the best and nobody was better than him, apart from maybe Brazilian Ronaldo, who was his idol growing up, and he would watch videos of him and try to replicate in his council estate. If you watch a highlight reel of his best goals he was incredible."
Honigstein: "What makes him unique among the strikers is his technique, You could see elements of martial arts in his goals. No-one scores goals like that."
The first Englishman on the list, although the third to have represented Manchester United - it's the Old Trafford outfit's record goalscorer, Wayne Rooney.

Honigstein: "I don't think there is anyone who would've watched English football at that time [early in his career] and not been enthralled by his game. The only downside is the combination of injuries and not the most professional lifestyle meant he did not fulfil his potential. He could've been Messi."
Gianni Infantino has been president of Fifa since 2016 and is standing for re-election for a third time
Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima will take on incumbent Gianni Infantino in next year's Fifa presidential election.
World football's governing body has confirmed the three candidates for the election, which will take place at the Fifa Congress in Morocco on 18 March.
European football's governing body Uefa only identified its candidate Diallo fewer than 48 hours before Wednesday's deadline.
French Football Federation (FFF) president Diallo, 63, received the unanimous support of Uefa's executive committee.
Japan Football Association honorary president Tashima, 68, announced his intention to stand against Infantino, 56, earlier this month.
Tashima is a member of the Fifa Council and a former international footballer and coach.
Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega had also said he intended to stand but was not named as a candidate by Fifa on Thursday.

A late and surprise choice, Diallo said: "I have the experience, the convictions and the values which offer a credible alternative...I'm entering this campaign not just to provide a different voice, but to win."
But he is not the Frenchman some believe Uefa really wanted, as it tries to remove Infantino in the wake of his failed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Senior figures in European football had hoped to persuade Arsene Wenger - Fifa's head of global development - to stand against his own boss. Some felt that only he possessed the credibility to pose a serious threat to Infantino's plans for a fourth term.
But after the former Arsenal manager chose not to proceed, Uefa had no choice but to seek an alternative.
So just how credible a challenger is Diallo? Does Infantino's position appear unassailable? And how could he still be stopped from winning another term?
Japan's Tashima to stand against Infantino for Fifa presidency
An administrator who has worked in French football since 1992 and became FFF president in 2023, Diallo is not a household name. But he has already shown he is prepared to stand up to Infantino.
In September, Diallo claimed he had "seriously damaged the image and unity of football", and said "trust has been broken" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) sell-off plot.
According to Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister, Diallo is a "candidate who can instigate real, meaningful and lasting reform" within the governing body.

"We've always made it very clear that our objectives and motivations are driving culture change. That means wide-ranging, systemic reform of football governance rather than simply the replacement of an individual leader," McAllister told BBC Sport.

"I've known Philippe since we were both elected to Uefa's executive committee, and he's an intelligent, honest, sharp-minded football person with an impressive experience of governance in one of the world's football power-houses. Most importantly, he is a person of integrity... Philippe is a fantastic advocate for the change agenda that football needs, and I know his campaign will reflect that."
Infantino remains the favourite to win a majority of the 211 votes, and is thought to have the support of most of Africa (54 members), Asia (47) and South America (10).

However, Uefa hopes that Diallo - whose father was a Senegalese boxing champion who represented France in the 1960 Olympics - could enjoy support in parts of Africa and beyond. He claims he already has the backing of countries beyond Europe.
Laura McAllister is a former captain of the Wales women's football team

While most of Europe's national associations are expected to vote for Diallo, it is clear that he was not Uefa's first choice. "I wasn't initially a candidate, but the insistence of my European colleagues led me to accept the offer," he admitted.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/athletics/ar: Peres Jepchirchir won the 2026 Sydney marathon by three minutes and 40 seconds
Reigning world marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir has been banned for three years for a doping violation.

The 33-year-old, who also won Olympic gold in 2021, was provisionally suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) in October after an out-of-competition sample tested positive for erythropoietin (EPO).
The sample was collected in Kenya prior to Jepchirchir winning the Sydney Marathon on 30 August 2026 and returned an adverse finding on 17 September.

She is one of three high-profile Kenyan athletes to have been sanctioned. Veronica Loleo has also been banned for three years after admitting using EPO, while Ronald Korir has received a six-year ban after failing to explain abnormalities found in his biological passport.
EPO is a natural substance produced within the kidneys that stimulates the creation of new red blood cells.
If injected, it increases the amount of red blood cells, which carry oxygen to the muscles, in the blood stream but is only detectable in urine or blood for a short window of time.
Jepchirchir's other major wins came at the New York Marathon in 2021, the Boston Marathon in 2022 and the London Marathon in 2024.
While she denied using EPO, she signed an admission of violations form and accepted disqualification of all her competitive results since 17 July 2026.

"The Kenyan authorities have made a lot of progress in the fight against doping in the last five years, but these cases highlight that there is still a long way to go," said Brett Clothier, chief executive of the AIU.

"The Kenyan government is aware of the current situation and has committed to further strengthen the Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya and take action to address the criminal networks that facilitate doping within the country.
"We will discuss the details behind these commitments with the Kenyan government in the coming months."
In September, Kenya was awarded the right to host the 2029 World Athletics Championships, with London and Rome missing out.

The decision increased scrutiny of the country's efforts to tackle a long-running doping problem, with more than 140 Kenyan athletes, predominantly distance runners, having been suspended by the AIU since 2017.

Last month Witold Banka, president of the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada), told BBC Sport that Kenya must demonstrate it can be a "clean" home of athletics if it is to retain its credibility leading up to the 2029 event.
Jepchirchir's ban will deepen scepticism towards Kenyan athletes, including those competing cleanly, and further place the spotlight on athletics administrators and the government.
She is the second high-profile Kenyan athlete to be banned for doping in the past two years, following 2019 world champion Ruth Chepngetich, who was sanctioned last year .
The timing is particularly damaging. Jepchirchir's ban comes two months after Kenya won the bid to become the first African country to host the World Athletics Championships in 2029.

Kenya's bid was built on its rich history as an athletics powerhouse, producing numerous World and Olympic champions in middle and long-distance running but doping scandals threaten to overshadow that legacy.
The suspension of another high-profile athlete, who has won Olympic, World and major marathon titles, reinforces concerns about the integrity of Kenyan athletics.

The AIU has previously said the country's cases are isolated with no evidence of systemic violations. Local anti-doping officials say testing, investigations and sanctions have been strengthened in recent years.
However, recurring cases involving elite athletes raise questions about whether deterrence, education and efforts to prosecute those facilitating doping are keeping pace.

That's the message from Māori artist and rugby league supporter Charles Williams, who told RNZ the celebrations surrounding the Rugby League World Cup are about something much bigger than what happens on the field.
Despite the Kiwis suffering a big loss to the Kangaroos in the final, across Tāmaki Makaurau and beyond, supporters took to the streets waving flags, singing and celebrating their whakapapa.

At the centre of many of those celebrations was Williams (Ngāti Kahungunu ki te Wairoa, Te Whakatohea, Tūhoe, Ngāpuhi), who organised a series of parades to bring people together in support of the Kiwis.
The idea was inspired by the passion of Tongan supporters during the 2017 Rugby League World Cup.

"2017, the Tongan fans really took fandom to another level. So they went all out and they were basically riding solo. During that 2017 campaign, we saw them all over the streets of South Auckland, where I live.
"Post World Cup, I went to Tonga, did an art project over there, got to meet them and got to see even more the fan base there and how crazy they are.
"Come 2026, I really wanted us to kind of just get off the couch, really get out of the house. Let's be inspired by our whānau from Tonga, Samoa."
Williams approached New Zealand Rugby League with the idea and rallied friends to help bring the parades to life.
It began with around 50 people gathering at Māngere Bridge during the first week of the tournament. By the second week, the crowds had grown to hundreds, and the flags kept coming.

"I've noticed in this World Cup, there's been more of an emphasis on, yeah, hey, I'm from Tonga, Samoa, Cook Islands, Fiji, Papua New Guinea, so on and so forth. And even guys who are not a part of the Rugby League World Cup are jumping in.

"Guys from Niue, all of a sudden you got yellow flags all over the streets. They want to be proud of themselves and everyone wants to be proud of themselves. They want to stand up and go, 'Hey, here I am, here we are and we're from here.'
"And that's awesome, you know, and I love it. And I want people to really be proud of where they're from."
But the parades also prompted a bigger reflection for Williams about how Māori come together as a people, and how those gatherings are perceived by others.
Māori flags, including the Tino Rangatiratanga flag and He Whakaputanga flag, are often seen at hīkoi and protests, where communities gather to advocate for their rights, identity and rangatiratanga.
Williams said some people mocked the parades online, questioning whether supporters were protesting or taking part in a hīkoi.
And while he understands why people might make that association, he said the celebrations offered a different opportunity to come together under the same flag.
"One thing I've been thinking about for a little bit is how do we celebrate as a people? So we're kind of like known as the 'fighting people'.

"A lot of the comments mocking us were, oh, are you guys protesting? You know what I mean? And it's like, cool. "You know, I understand why you say that, because literally, we are always protesting. But it's been the first time, not the first time ever, but it's like the first time I've seen thousands of people with a Tino Rangatiratanga flag, happy, celebrating, and we're not actually fighting for anything.
"We're not trying to like get anything. It's just like, bro, we're just happy."
"We're under this flag. We're under this banner. And to celebrate, it's just been like, finally, we're just like, we're just happy."

The All Blacks say they're happy with the way hip and knee drop tackles are being officiated after Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus was suspended for criticising match officials.

World Rugby has banned the 54-year-old for six games for his post-match comments after South Africa's 21-19 defeat to France last weekend, in which he questioned whether officials were manipulating the game.
Erasmus, who has a long track record of publicly criticising match officials , believes they failed to notice, or ignored, up to 17 illegal tackles in Paris.

Hip tackles (a defender putting his weight on the lower limbs of an attacker in the act of bringing him down), and knee tackles (a defender starting the act of making a tackle while on one or both of his knees) was made illegal by World Rugby on 1 November.
All Blacks wing Leroy Carter required ankle surgery after being caught in a hip tackle during his team's Bledisloe Cup victory at Eden Park in October.
"The TMO (television match official) doesn't come in once. I'm not saying he's wrong. I'm saying if he didn't see it, it must be a technology problem," Erasmus said after the test.
"If he saw it and he decided not to act on it, is that not match-fixing? Is that not interfering with the outcome of a game?"
Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus will miss this weekend's test against Ireland.

South Africa Rugby has confirmed Erasmus will request a full misconduct hearing in order to "contextualise his comments and assure the panel that it was not his intention to allege that any match official had acted with ulterior motives".

The All Blacks also believe some illegal tackles went unpunished in last Sunday's 35-28 loss to Wales in Cardiff, with stand-in captain Beauden Barrett heard on multiple occasions asking referee Pierre Brousset about the hosts making hip drop tackles.
However, All Blacks hooker Asafo Aumua, speaking ahead of his side's clash with England at Twickenham on Sunday, said officials were largely getting it right.
"I think there were a few missed ones on the weekend, but that wasn't going to really change the result in the game," Aumua said.
"I feel like they're [match officials] doing enough, we've just got to be a bit more accurate in our tackles."
Aumua said he didn't think players intentionally made hip or knee drop tackles, but added they could be hard to avoid in a sport as dynamic as rugby.
"On the weekend, I felt like I'd nearly done maybe two [hip drop tackles], but not on purpose," Aumua said.
"I just got beaten on the outside and grabbed them and ended up swinging around, so I just let go."
Aumua said the best way to minimise illegal tackles was to focus on technique.
"Just getting in front [of the attacker] and trying to get them going back instead of swinging around."
As it stands, Erasmus is set to miss the Springboks clash with Ireland this Sunday and their Nations Championship playoff match the following weekend.
The ban is set to expire during next year's Rugby Championship, meaning Erasmus will be back in the hot seat in time for their World Cup title defence in Australia, which starts next October.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmgr: Google has refused a government request to remove a YouTube video posted by jailed rapist Russell Brand's wife in which he claims his innocence, Whitehall sources have told the BBC.
The Prison Service of England and Wales submitted the request. A Ministry of Justice (MoJ) spokesperson said "it was only right" to ask for content that was "distressing for victims" to be removed.
The disgraced comedian is currently in prison after being sentenced to 10-and-a-half years following his conviction for rape and three counts of sexual assault.
Google told BBC News in a statement it was "aware of the new content and our teams are investigating".
It added: "We suspended Russell Brand's channel from the YouTube Partner Program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then."
On Sunday, Brand's wife Laura shared a video on their YouTube channel and read out a message from Brand in which he claimed: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."
The MoJ spokesperson added that while "removal ultimately depends on the platform's own terms", the department strongly believes "YouTube should remove this content".
The Prison Service of England and Wales formally requested that the video be removed on the basis that they believed it was offensive to Brand's victims and had reached a substantial audience.
The BBC was initially told a minister had met Google to request the deactivation of Brand's account.

The MoJ later clarified the request had focused on the controversial video, and it is now understood a minister did not meet Google and the request was made via an established mechanism the prison service has with tech companies to request deletion of material.
The BBC has been told that Google declined the request, saying that its rules had not been broken.
However, speaking on BBC Breakfast, housing minister Matthew Pennycook described the video as "abhorrent" and said the government remained in "close dialogue" with Google.

Jess Phillips, the former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the government "doesn't have the power to enforce that this video is taken down".

"It relies on YouTube, in this instance ... to do the right thing, which is a much, much broader argument about whether Ofcom codes that are in the Online Safety Act are there actually to protect women," she said.
An Ofcom spokesperson said in a statement that while the current guidance "pushes platforms to go above and beyond their legal duties... ultimately parliament chose to make it voluntary".
"Any changes to the legislation to make it mandatory would be a matter for government and parliament," they added.

Phillips, describing Brand as an "absolute narcissist", suggested it was "very likely" that the government would look at introducing a second online safety act to address gaps in the current regulatory framework.
"Before, we haven't had prisoners who had massive YouTube followings," she said. "This is an entirely new era."
Brand's message prompted an investigation into whether he had broken prison rules.

Downing Street previously called the message "clearly appalling", adding: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances."
Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the case was being "urgently investigated, and I expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules".

Prisoners' phone conversations are routinely recorded, but not necessarily listened to by prison authorities. If Brand is found to have breached the rules, possible repercussions could include a temporary phone ban or live monitoring of his calls.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6eq: The band have become known for their energetic live performances and interwoven four-part harmonies
Westside Cowboy have been announced as BBC Introducing Artist of the Year 2026.
Jimmy Bradbury, Reuben Haycocks, Aoife Anson O'Connell and Paddy Murphy formed the band in Manchester in 2023 and have since rocketed from the pub circuit to some of the UK's biggest festivals.

The award is presented to an up-and-coming artist or band who has, with the support of BBC Introducing, made a significant impact and has previously been won by Olivia Dean, Myles Smith and Tom Grennan.
Murphy, from Longridge in Lancashire, said the win put them in "good company", with Bradbury, from Shropshire, adding that it was "very flattering".

BBC Introducing supports new musical talent across the UK , providing a platform to propel new artists on to the local and national stage through 30 Introducing shows, three national radio shows and six shows across BBC Radio 1, Radio 1Xtra, Radio 2, 6Music, Radio 3 and Asian Network.
About 72,000 tracks from emerging UK artists supported by BBC Introducing make it on to the airwaves each year.

Westside Cowboy uploaded their debut single I've Never Met Anyone I Thought I Could Really Love (Until I Met You) to the Introducing platform in November 2024 and had their first play on radio within hours.
Murphy and Bradbury were surprised with the award during a radio interview
The four-piece played in various other bands before coming together to form Westside Cowboy.
Haycocks, O'Connell, and Murphy had met at Manchester's Royal Northern College of Music in 2021 and later got to know Bradbury after meeting him in the nearby Johnny Roadhouse music shop.

Murphy and Bradbury played in surf-rock trio Katz, while Murphy and Haycocks both worked together in noise-pop trio, DieKaiDie, but it was when Bradbury, who was working in the music shop repairing guitars, asked the others if they wanted to start a new band that Westside Cowboy's journey began.

By the time their second single, Shells, was released in April 2025, they had been been selected to play the BBC Introducing stage at Glastonbury Festival, and the song was put on the BBC 6Music playlist.

Their meteoric rise saw seen them appear on BBC music show Later... with Jools Holland in June and their debut album It Goes On was released on Island Records in August, peaking at number five in the UK charts.
Westside Cowboy reminisced about the early days on BBC Radio Manchester
Thanking the Introducing network and listeners for their support, Murphy said it was "really cool to be recognised for the music you make".
"We say this a lot, so apologies if we sound like a broken record, [but] it's funny with this band because... we started it with so little pretence or plan," he said.
"So whenever people give us something cool like [this award], it's all a bit surreal because it still feels like a weekend project that we now just get to do way more regularly.
Westside Cowboy formed in 2023, having played together in other bands
William Wolstenholme, presenter and producer of BBC Introducing in Lancashire & Cumbria, gave the band their first play and said he remembers messaging them to upload the track.
"Over the past two years, Westside Cowboy have become surely the most exciting band in Manchester, and therefore the country," he said.
"They've fast-tracked from the sweaty pubs of the city's student music scene to many of the most famous venues in the country.
"It's a rise whose speed can scarcely be believed, and one that has shocked much of the music industry."
He said the band's obvious camaraderie was one of their main selling points.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crwy: Harry Styles will compete with Cher for the weekend's most flamboyant outfit

The veteran US pop icon will play the coveted Sunday afternoon "legends" slot, which is often considered a fourth headline set. It will be her only UK festival appearance of the year.

Tickets for the festival sold out in just 42 minutes last month , with demand particularly high after the event took a year off in 2026.
Cher is bound to draw a huge crowd to hear hits like Turn Back Time, Believe and I Got You Babe

"We are so happy to be coming back after our fallow year and, as we head into winter after that peaceful period, we wanted to give you an early musical taster of what's to come at Glastonbury 2027 with this spread of incredible artists," said organiser Emily Eavis.
"We can't wait to see you down here on Worthy Farm in June for some much-needed good times!"
The gates will open at Worthy Farm in Somerset to 200,000 fans on Wednesday 23 June, with music on the main stages kicking off on Friday 25 June.
Tickets prices are at an all-time high of £408, including a £5 booking fee per ticket.
Festival organiser Emily Eavis watched Sam Fender's set from the side of the stage in 2022

He last played in 2022, immediately before Billie Eilish, and fought back tears as thousands of fans chanted along to hits like Seventeen Going Under and Hypersonic Missiles.

Fender is expected to release a new album ahead of his Glastonbury slot, which will land in the middle of his catchily-titled Proper Massive Stadium Tour.
Billie Eilish was the youngest solo act to headline Glastonbury when she topped the bill in 2022
Harry Styles will take the Pyramid Stage crown on the Saturday.
It comes amid acclaim for his euphoric and athletic Together Together tour, which largely focuses on the understated dance anthems of his fourth album Kiss All The Time. Disco Occasionally.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6x2: Singer Julio Iglesias is facing an investigation by Spain's national court over allegations he sexually abused and assaulted two female former staff members
Two women, who worked for the 83-year-old in the Caribbean, have accused him of abuse which they say took place in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic in 2021.
The announcement comes after Spanish prosecutors dropped an inquiry into the claims earlier this year after concluding that they lacked jurisdiction because the alleged crimes took place abroad.
Iglesias, who has been a household name in Spain since the 1960s and has sold millions of records worldwide, has previously denied the allegations .

But in a statement published on Wednesday , external (in Spanish), national court Judge Antonio Piña said the account given in the complaint, alongside preliminary evidence provided, justified opening criminal proceedings.
He added that the investigation would cover parts of the complaint relating to potential crimes against sexual freedom, as well as assault and degrading treatment.

But the court will not investigate claims made in the lawsuit of human trafficking or crimes against workers' rights. Piña said these allegations were dismissed after he looked into the hiring of the women and found there was "no deception or artifice involved".
Piña said the former employees had been summoned to testify in person on 3 February.
The announcement comes after Spain's public prosecutor's office shifted its position last month, saying it now believed the court had jurisdiction to investigate the allegations.
In its statement, the national court said Spanish law sets out that courts can hear cases of crimes committed abroad by Spanish citizens provided certain conditions are met.
The allegations against Iglesias first emerged in a joint three-year investigation between Spanish newspaper El Diario , external and television network Univision news, published in January.
In that investigation, the two women were identified as a domestic worker and a physical therapist, who described alleged sexual abuse and degrading working conditions.
The domestic worker, whose name was changed to Rebeca in the reports, said Iglesias would regularly call her to his room at the end of the day and would touch her inappropriately without consent.

Rebeca, a Dominican who was 22 when the alleged events took place, also alleged that Iglesias had forced her to take part in threesomes with another female member of staff. She also described the singer slapping her in the face and grabbing her genitals.

The other woman, a Venezuelan physical therapist named as Laura in the article, said Iglesias had touched her breasts and kissed her on the mouth against her will. She added that he constantly threatened to fire her, controlled how much food she ate and asked her about when her period was due.
Rebeca and Laura filed an initial legal complaint in January against Iglesias for sexual assault and human trafficking.
In a response to the allegations in January, Iglesias said , external : "I deny having abused, coerced, or disrespected any woman. These accusations are absolutely false and deeply sadden me."

On Wednesday, the court said the lawsuit had been accepted based on evidence provided in the complaint. This included a photograph of one of the complainants, showing a bruise on her arm that was "consistent with the possibility of her being grabbed forcefully".

It added that the same photo showed "two marks on one of her thighs that could correspond to a human bite", which the complainant said were "a consequence of her forced participation in acts of a sexual nature".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm4g: Freja, who "didn't expect to be chosen" as the winner, beat more than 1,000 entries from across the UK

Her design will be the official BBFC black card, which displays the age rating and classification details of the film before every cinema showing.
Freja's winning design will be shown as the official BBFC black card before every UK cinema screening

Freja and her mum attended a fan screening event for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on The Reaping in London

Actor Ralph Fiennes said: "It looks wonderful, it's really amazing, I love it."
Freja only started oil painting three years ago, but her mum says she has always been a creative person

Marie said her daughter spent more than a month on the piece and worked until the day of the deadline after she "locked in for a whole weekend" to get it done.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9vg: Reviews of the latest Hunger Games film have seen it dismissed as a "surreally awful prequel" and "a tortuous, costly mess" by some critics - but called "surprisingly strong" and "one of the best films in the series" by others.
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is the sixth movie in the franchise, and tells the origin story of a teenage Haymitch Abernathy - who was played as an adult by Woody Harrelson.

In a one-star review, the Guardian called the film , external "overwrought and boring", and said it "has no actual interest and no authentic reason to exist, other than to gouge an income stream out of its fanbase".
But the Wrap praised its , external "memorable performances, intoxicating style and horrifying commentary", adding: "When the dust settles it may even be the Hunger Games that holds up best."
Sunrise on the Reaping is set 24 years before the first Hunger Games film, and 40 years after the previous prequel, 2023's The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.
"This prequel lands at some mid-point between Ballad and Hunger Games, which puts it on an immediately odd footing," Empire said in a three-star review , external .
"It can't escape the sense of feeling supplementary. It's an enjoyable-enough diversion, but essentially a footnote with aspirations."

Screen Daily called it , external an "underwhelming prequel", which "suffers from a lack of compelling characters" and "feels oddly incidental - a drab afterthought rather than a crucial new chapter".
The film's all-star cast includes Ralph Fiennes, Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace and Maya Hawke alongside Joseph Zada as the 16-year-old Abernathy.
IndieWire , external said Zada's performance is "charming enough", but "his character lacks the gravitational charisma or arc that, say, Jennifer Lawrence brought to the original films".
The movie feels "a little bit like a cold cash grab rather than a necessary deepening of the series' lore" and is "a dreary slog", IndieWire's critic wrote.

The New York Times , external also used the word "slog", adding: "One really misses the guiding presence of Jennifer Lawrence, who had the raw pathos to both ground and expand a world in a way many younger stars often can't.
"In Sunrise, we're instead left with fleeting moments in which Plemons or Ralph Fiennes (playing the evil President Snow) briefly elevate the film. They seem to be trapped in this dystopia too."
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping will be released this weekend
However, the Hollywood Reporter , external was more enthusiastic about both the film and Zada's performance, calling it a "star-making turn".
Its critic concluded: "Sunrise on the Reaping is a return, after the disappointing Songbirds and Snakes, to the spirit of the first movies."
And Time Out's four-star review , external said the film is "as strong as any" of the other movies, and "certainly a major step up from 2023's drab prequel The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes".

Danika Priim, 42, has been charged with carrying out the alleged sexual assault in the toilets at Horsforth Cricket Club in Leeds on 22 July 2022.
Her accuser, who cannot be named for legal reasons, previously told a trial at Leeds Crown Court how Priim twice reached up her dress and grabbed her underwear.
Keighley-based Priim, who previously represented Bradford Bulls, Leeds Rhinos and England, including at the 2017 World Cup, denies one count of sexual assault. The trial continues.
Two of the complainant's friends told the court they also witnessed what happened in the toilet but, on Wednesday, Priim told the jury she was never in the toilets with the three women.
Prosecutor Chloe Hudson put it to Priim that there were only two alternatives – either she was lying or the complainant and her two friends were lying.
The defendant agreed she was not suggesting that it was an accident, or the woman had invited her to touch her, or it was a joke.
Priim told the jury she was never in the toilets with the complainant, adding: "I did not touch (her) in the toilets at all."
Hudson said to her: "What you must be saying is that these three got together to make completely false allegations about you."
Priim responded: "It's the biggest question I have – it's the why."
The prosecutor asked the defendant about how the complainant demonstrated to the jury how she was grabbed.
She added: "I'm also a very happy heterosexual woman. I'm with a man. I live with a man."
The prosecutor said: "The truth is that you sexually assaulted (the woman), didn't you?"
Danika Priim, right, represented England at the 2017 World Cup
Hudson asked Priim whether she thought the complainant and her two friends had colluded in a "witch hunt against you".
Stood in the witness box wearing a chunky light brown cardigan and a cream-and-black scarf, Priim replied: "I believe they have."
On Tuesday, the complainant described how Priim "walked straight up to me and put her hand up my skirt and grabbed hold of my pants and my private parts".
The woman said she asked the defendant what she was doing, "then she did it again, grinning at me, and walked off".
One of the complainant's friends told the jury how she witnessed Priim put her hand up the woman's skirt.
She told the court: "I recall seeing her remove her hand, laughed about it and then repeated it.

Giving evidence on Wednesday, Priim said she only went to the toilet once during her time at the cricket club, and produced a photograph she took of her and two friends in there, to help the jury with timings.
She said she drove to the venue and was drinking soft drinks until later when she had one pint.
Asked about the police getting involved following the allegation, she said: "It absolutely broke me."
Since retiring from the game in 2021 Priim has appeared on BBC, Channel 4 and Sky Sports as a pundit, reporter and commentator.
