https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm89: The legal action against Natural Resources Wales landed in the High Court
River campaigners are taking on Wales' environmental regulator in the High Court over what they believe is a "regulatory gap" that risks pollution from poultry farms in two rivers.

River Action UK has accused Natural Resources Wales (NRW) of not doing enough to assess or address any risk to local rivers and and other water bodies when plans for three farms in Powys were approved last year.
It follows years of debate over the alleged impact of chicken farming on rivers such as the Wye and Severn - in an area dubbed the UK's "poultry capital" .
NRW said it would be inappropriate to comment ahead of the court case, but that it would "participate fully in the legal process".
The case is about plans to increase the capacity of three Powys farms by a combined 336,900 chickens, bringing the total to 522,000.
Two of the farms, Rhosddu and Llanshay, are in the River Severn catchment while Neuadd Isaf is in the River Wye catchment.
Campaigners said the Severn was showing "signs of strain" with regular algal blooms, brown algae smothering the riverbed.
The three poultry units in Powys are located within river catchments including the River Wye
Campaigners' concerns have centred around the birds' manure becoming a pollutant when it is spread on fields and leaches into rivers.
Nutrient-rich agricultural run-off can contribute to algal blooms, turning rivers green and smothering wildlife.
Following a consultation, NRW approved permit variations in November 2025, allowing the three poultry units to expand.
Rather than keep and spread the manure on site, the farms' operators said they would export it for use or processing elsewhere.

River Action argued NRW wrongly concluded it had no legal power under the Environmental Permitting Regulations 2016 to assess the potential environmental impacts of this off-site manure management, or to take action to prevent or mitigate pollution arising from it.
Emma Dearnaley, head of legal at River Action, argues there is a "regulatory gap" in the management of off-site manure
Campaigners set up a chicken-themed protest outside the High Court hearing in Llandrindod Wells on Tuesday.

"River Action will argue that Natural Resources Wales has the power to address and assess the impact of that manure on the environment and, as the specialist regulator, should be lawfully deciding how to use that power when operating the permitting regime," said Julia Eriksen, of solicitors Leigh Day, representing River Action.
The organisation insisted NRW could put controls on the farm's permit to reduce or remove the risk of manure causing pollution.
Campaigners believe the birds' manure will spread on fields and into rivers, causing harm

Emma Dearnaley, head of legal at River Action, said NRW "decided that it didn't have the power to look at what would happen when a lot of the manure would go offsite" when the plans were approved in 2025.
"That matters because more chickens means more muck, and that needs to go somewhere and someone has to deal with it," she said.
"So this case is all about making NRW realise that it does have the power to deal with it."

An NRW spokesperson said: "As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment on matters that are before the court. We will continue to participate fully in the legal process and await the court's determination."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqly: Watch: William and Catherine walk green carpet in Mumbai for Earthshot Prize
The Prince and Princess of Wales have said environmental innovators are changing the lives of future generations as they celebrated this year's winners of the Earthshot Prize.
Five award-winners were named at a ceremony in Mumbai, India, and will each receive £1m to scale up their projects.
One of the winners was a country - with Bhutan being recognised for its environmental policies that help to safeguard water supplies for nearly a fifth of the world's population.

Indian cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar, actor Rami Malek and Bollywood stars Alia Bhatt and Sonam Kapoor were among those who attended the ceremony, which saw performances from Take That and Bridgerton's Simone Ashley.
The annual event, founded by Prince William and now in its sixth year, was hosted by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known film makers.

Prince William was joined by Catherine at the ceremony as the royal couple continued their first official overseas trip together in four years. Catherine's cancer treatment has limited the amount she has travelled internationally.
They arrived on the event's green carpet wearing outfits celebrating Indian fashion.

Prince William wore a bespoke Bandhgala, a classic Indian formal jacket, while Catherine was dressed in an Anarkali dress by Mahima Mahajan made from handwoven silk Georgette with traditional Banarasi gold detailing.

During his speech, Prince William said this decade was the moment when positive change becomes irreversible" and remarked that history was "not written by challenges alone", but also by those who rose to meet them.
He added that "around the world, we are witnessing human ingenuity on a remarkable scale".
Separately, Catherine highlighted the "hope" represented by entrepreneurs, organisations and scientists tackling the environmental crisis.
The princess, who presented an award, also said: "Just as the natural world finds ways to adapt and flourish, so too can we, when we nurture new ideas and give them the opportunity to grow.
"The people we're celebrating tonight are a huge part of that story. Their work will inspire and create seismic change that will improve lives for generations to come."
William and Catherine talk with guests during the awards ceremony in Mumbai
The royal couple also spoke to those performing, which included Take That
There are five Earthshots, or goals, for which an award is given: Protect and Restore Nature; Clean Our Air; Revive Our Oceans; Build a Waste-Free World; and Fix Our Climate.
Five winners were chosen from a list of 15 finalists who attended Tuesday's awards ceremony.

Protect and Restore Nature: Bhutan, the country that helps to protect the water security of 1.6 billion people across South Asia and has a national nature coalition that aims to revive forests and rivers by restoring 50,000 hectares of damaged land

Build a Waste-Free World: PFAS-Free France, a national campaign that helped secure landmark legislation banning 'forever chemicals' in France by 2030, and hopes to extend the ban to more major countries
Revive Our Oceans: Niue Ocean Wide Trust, the Pacific island's scheme that has safeguarded marine life by investing in conservation to fund the long-term protection of its vast waters

Clean Our Air: Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, a scheme rolling out up to one million electric rickshaws across India with the aim to drasitically cut one of the world's largest sources of on-road air pollution
Fix Our Climate: Ørsted, a global energy company that has cut its direct carbon emissions by more than 98% by transforming from being highly coal-intensive to a leader in offshore wind
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr5y: The contaminated Mobuoy dump is thought to cover more than 100 acres of land
More than £160m is needed to clean up and maintain one of Europe's largest illegal landfill sites, government officials have said.
The contaminated Mobuoy dump at Campsie in County Londonderry, discovered and shut down in 2013, was used to bury thousands of tonnes of rubbish at a site spanning more than 100 acres.
Last year, two businessmen were jailed for their part in the operation.
Northern Ireland's Environment Minister Andrew Muir said his department had now received an updated cost estimate of £161m for the clean-up over a 30-year period.
Muir described what happened at Mobuoy as "an absolute scandal" and said "the community rightly expects and deserves remediation of the site".
He is now seeking a meeting with the Finance Minister John O'Dowd to discuss how the work will be paid for - with funding from Westminster a possibility.
Once the finances are agreed, they will work towards appointing a contractor.
Andrew Muir says it could take a generation to clean up the Mobuoy dump in County Londonderry
Investigations indicate an estimated 1.6m tonnes of waste was present at the site and 627,000 tonnes of that was believed to have been dumped illegally.
The Mobuoy site is beside the River Faughan, which supplies a significant proportion of Derry's drinking water but officials have not found any contamination to it.
The area of polluted ground stretches to about 100 acres, or the equivalent of about 65-70 football pitches.
"This is a complicated project, as you'll understand, given the complexity of the site," Muir told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme on Tuesday, .
The minister said he took environmental protection very seriously and would continue to push for the establishment of an independent environmental protection agency.
"One of the massive lessons that needs to be learned from the Mobuoy site is the need for stronger environmental protections, so people have confidence that our environment is being looked after."
The site, located on the outskirts of the city, is a former recycling plant
Muir said the next assembly election was fast approaching in May, so he understood there might be some concerns about the potential costs involved.
"I want to finish this mandate with a degree of certainty for the local community, so we have a road map here for remediation," he said.
Muir said the drinking water was tested regularly to ensure it was safe and that he would continue to work with all agencies to provide the local community with greater assurances about the site.
Muir said the Mobuoy site remained in private ownership, but they were "actively" considering ways of transferring it.
One option is vesting, which allows government departments to obtain compulsory and legal ownership of land through a court order.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/c: A single meteor streaks across the starry night sky during the annual Leonid meteor shower
The Leonid meteor shower reaches its peak on Tuesday night, giving UK sky gazers their best chance to see it this year.
The celestial spectacle runs until 30 November, but the greatest activity is expected on the night of Tuesday 17 November, into the early hours of Wednesday.
There could be the chance to spot up to 10-15 meteors per hour.
The shower is made up of dust particles from the Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which leaves a trail of debris as it follows its path around the Sun.
These particles enter the Earth's atmosphere at up to 44 miles (71km) per second, meaning these streaks of light are the fastest meteors in the sky.
Experts advise finding a safe, dark location away from sources of light pollution such as street lights.
The meteors will be visible with the naked eye, with no binoculars or telescope required.
However, giving your eyes some time to adapt to the dark, perhaps 20 or 30 minutes, will give you the best chance of spotting them.
A wide open space is the best place to be, giving a full view of the night sky.

Meteors could be visible anywhere but the Leonids' radiant, the point from which they seem to appear, will, as the name suggests, be around the head of the constellation Leo, meaning this is the best part of the sky to focus your gaze. Leo does not rise until around midnight, so the best time to look is after midnight and in the hours before dawn.
As with all celestial spectacles, clear skies will be a must.

Viewing conditions could be particularly good around the peak. The Moon will set at around 23:30 GMT on Tuesday, meaning its reflected light is less likely to spoil the view in the hours after midnight.
The best chance of seeing the Leonids will be in the far north of Scotland, including Orkney and Shetland, where cloud is expected to be well broken with only a small chance of a passing shower.
Parts of Northern Ireland, Wales, the Midlands and southern England will also have clear spells at times but there will be periods of cloudier weather and some splashes of rain.
In Northern Ireland, the Midlands and North Wales, the best chance of clear breaks will be earlier in the night.
Much of Scotland away from the far north, and northern England, will have limited opportunities. A few places may see the odd gap in the cloud but for most it will be cloudy and damp.

Work to gain access to land for a housing development and a new "super cycleway" has resulted in "environmental vandalism", councillors have said.

The trees and hedgerows were cut back on land next to the Oxford Road

According to Bellway, the trees and hedges were cut down between 26 October and 6 November to "create access" to the site planned for housing, as well as to "facilitate" the work for the cycleway.
The proposals include "significant landscaping and ecological enhancements" as well as 50% affordable housing and "other infrastructure", it said.
Middleton, the lead member for housing and greener communities at Cherwell District Council, said outline planning permission did not give the developer "unrestricted permission to carry out works".
He also said its actions were "nonsensical" and premature, given the cycle path was not "imminent".
"If all they needed was access, why have they ripped out an entire hedgerow?" he said.
"We knew some of this was going to be taken out, but it's the scale of it that's really impacted people and sent shock waves across the local community."

India have edged New Zealand 3-2 in a closely contested opening match of their three-test hockey series in Auckland, with the Black Sticks mounting a fightback before the visitors held on for the win.
Earlier today, the Indian Armed Forces team also faced the New Zealand Defence Force, with the visitors winning the match 4-1.
The match at Lloyd Elsmore Hockey Stadium is part of a series marking 100 years of sporting ties between India and New Zealand, which began with an Indian Army hockey team's tour of Aotearoa in 1926.
The team was the first Indian hockey side to tour overseas and the first Indian sporting team to visit New Zealand.
It included Dhyan Chand, who would go on to become one of the sport's most celebrated players.
The New Zealand Hockey Association contributed £500 towards the tour, which proved an overwhelming success, helping promote hockey and attracting unprecedented crowds.
An estimated 25,000 people attended the third and final test between New Zealand and the Indian Army team at Eden Park – a record crowd for a hockey match in New Zealand that still stands today.
The match at Lloyd Elsmore Hockey Stadium today is part of a series marking 100 years of sporting ties between India and New Zealand.
A century later, the two countries are marking that milestone through a series of hockey fixtures.
The Slumberzone Indian Centenary Hockey Series features five matches involving a 25-member Indian contingent drawn from the country's army, navy and air force.
The team arrived in New Zealand earlier this month, with the tour opening with two matches in the Wellington region before moving to Auckland for three more fixtures.
These include two games against the New Zealand Defence Force and one against the New Zealand Indian Sports Association men's team.
The centenary fixtures also coincide with a separate three-match test series between the Black Sticks men and India's national side.
The remaining two tests are scheduled for 21 and 22 November at Lloyd Elsmore Hockey Stadium in Auckland.

All three matches are being broadcast on TVNZ+, with Hindi-language commentary also available, allowing Hindi-speaking audiences in New Zealand and overseas to follow the series in their preferred language.
The Hindi commentary is AI-assisted, using technology and capabilities made possible by TVNZ+'s replatforming earlier this year, according to TVNZ.
Hundreds of fans turned out for the first Auckland hockey test between the Black Sticks and India.
The centenary celebrations have extended beyond hockey, with sporting and cultural events held across five New Zealand cities – Auckland, Christchurch, Hamilton, Tauranga and Wellington.
The programme has featured cricket, football, lawn bowls, beach volleyball and other sporting exchanges, highlighting the growing connections between the two countries.
India's cricket team has won both limited-overs series against New Zealand, taking the five-match T20 series 3-2 and the one-day international series 3-1, with one ODI match abandoned due to rain.
The two sides began their two-match Test series at Wellington's Basin Reserve on Thursday.
In football, the All Whites beat India's national team 5-0 in Auckland and 3-0 in Christchurch to sweep their two-match friendly series.
India also won the three-match esports series against New Zealand 2-1, with the contest featuring eFootball and women's Clash Royale.

In lawn bowls, India came from behind to beat New Zealand 2-1 in their three-test series in Auckland. After losing the opening test, the visitors won the second 3-2 and sealed the series with a 4-1 victory in the deciding test.

"The situation remains dynamic, and assessments are ongoing," DOC Operations Manager, Kaitaia, Laree Furniss said.
The immediate priority was the welfare of the surviving whales, Furniss said.
The DOC was also working with marine mammal specialists to determine the most appropriate response.

The public was asked to stay clear of the stranding site to allow responders to work safely and minimise stress to the whales.
The iwi said the whales had come ashore at the northern end of the beach, also known as Te Oneroa-a-Tōhe.
Penetaui Kleskovic, of Te Aupōuri iwi, said efforts on the beach were being led by Te Aupōuri with support from neighbouring Te Hiku iwi.
He said the stranded whales were a range of sizes and ages, each weighing an estimated seven to 10 tonnes.
Kleskovic said the work underway on the beach this evening was specialist mahi, with experts from Ngātiwai and Te Uri o Hau helping with the customary processes that follow a whale stranding.
Just last month, a pod of around 15 rare pygmy killer whales stranded near Hukatere, further south on Ninety Mile Beach, with most dying despite the efforts of rescuers.

Farewell Spit has a fluffy new resident, with a pair of takahē welcoming the first chick to a habitat at the top of the South Island.

The Department of Conservation (DOC) introduced eight of the threatened native birds to the Onetahua Restoration Project in May, giving them a new home inside a 2000-hectare habitat surrounded by a 4km predator-resistant fence.

The chick's parents were not an established breeding pair when they arrived in May, so the chick hatching in October was a welcome surprise, DOC's Golden Bay operations manager Ross Trotter told Checkpoint .
"They weren't known to each other, so they were introduced to each other in the area we call Triangle Flat in Pūponga, and yeah, it's resulted in a chick being born," Trotter said.
"It's about six weeks old now, which is great that it's survived to this stage because they're pretty vulnerable in the early stages."
Some other pairs had tried to nest but had been less successful. One nest was washed away, and another pair had an infertile egg, Trotter said.
While a significant amount of work had gone into making the habitat safe for the birds, the chick was still vulnerable, he said.
"We're still doing a heavy trapping programme to remove more predators, and we'll just have more and more improvement the longer we go."
The chick's parents were keeping it well hidden at this stage to protect it, Trotter said.
DOC says people should stay on the tracks and give mum and dad the space they need for their chick.
"Once it gets a bit older, 8 to 12 weeks, it'll start to get out in the open and unfortunately that will open it up to predation [from] hawks and falcons.
"We have had people going to try and look for it, but it's way better if people just stay on the tracks and give them the space they need."
The new breeding pair of birds was likely to stick together for life, Trotter told Checkpoint .
"We'll work with Manawhenua Ki Mohua around what that might get called ... once we get to that age where we know it's going to survive."
Manawhenua Ki Mohua chair Margie Little said they were delighted the takahē chick had hatched five months after the species' relocation from Gouland Downs.
"Its presence restores the wairua and mauri of the taonga species to Onetahua."
Pest Free Onetahua project lead Corey Mosen said a huge amount of work had gone into preparing the area for takahē.
"There's some great habitat here, with plenty of lush green grass and good food for the birds.
"With all the pest control along with the new fence, we're giving them a much better chance."
"The next few months are really important, so we're continuing to work hard to give this little chick the best possible start."

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/education/268: The New Zealand Qualifications Authority will prepare a new NCEA level 2 English exam in just a week and a half, so students can resit it following major technical problems last week.

The process of creating an exam usually takes about 18 months, but NZQA chief executive Christian Hawkesby said the unusual step was necessary because analysis showed students had been adversely affected by the disruption.

"All of the information from the exam was saved both digitally and in paper and we've been able to analyse that information and it showed that there was a significant disruption which really couldn't be addressed in the usual ways that we do in other circumstances such as using derived grades," he said.
"This is an exceptional circumstance given it was a severe prolonged, nationwide disruption and that's what's meant we've had to take this very unusual step of a resit exam."
Hawkesby said the new exam would be offered on 4 December. Schools would contact students next week to ask if they wanted to sit it.
He said about 40,000 students were enrolled for the original exam, including about 37,500 for the digital version.
NZQA did not know how many students might choose to sit the new exam.

"We have already announced that affected students will receive whichever result is higher - their exam grade, or the derived grade which comes from their practice exams or other suitable evidence of learning throughout the year.

"We are also using the marking process to recognise all the evidence of students' knowledge in their responses and will be reviewing the grade distributions from both exams against previous years to check that students are treated fairly."
Hawkesby refused to answer questions about RM, the company that provided the exam platform.
The New Zealand English Teaching Association doubted many students would take up the offer to re-sit their level 2 English exam.
"There will be students who absolutely will show up because it is going to be really, really important to them," association president Pip Tinning said.
But she said most students would be eyeing up their final exam.

"Telling students now on the 4th of December you can come back and have another go at another English exam, which is a pretty intense exam for our young people ... I imagine the numbers aren't going to be huge."
About 40,000 students were sitting NCEA level 2 English on Thursday last week - many of them online - when the malfunction disrupted the exam, forcing many to revert to using paper exams.
On Tuesday, NZQA apologised for the disruption to another online exam, this time level 1 English, and said it would undertake a full independent review.
Education Minister Erica Stanford said Tuesday's disruption was much smaller than the English level 2 exam, but it was still disappointing after repeated assurances from NZQA and its IT provider.

"Since the first detection of bird flu in New Zealand on 15 July this year, MPI has received more than 3500 public reports, and has carried out more than 3180 tests," she said.

A man accused of sexual offending against four young boys can now be named as Christchurch man Tahu Paki.

Paki faces 18 charges including nine of sexual violation by unlawful sexual connection, two of attempted sexual violation by unlawful sexual violation, two of indecent assault on a young person under 16 and five charges of indecent assault. Paki denies the allegations.
On Thursday, the Court of Appeal released a judgment declining his leave to bring a second appeal against name suppression.
In March, Christchurch District Court Judge Michael Crosbie declined Paki's name suppression.
Judge Crosbie said Paki's application was premised on publication of his name causing extreme hardship to himself and his family.
Crosbie's judgment said the Crown opposed interim name suppression, submitting that none of the grounds relied on by Paki reached the level of "extreme hardship".

The Crown also said there were "positive reasons" for not allowing suppression to continue, including that suppression of his name was "impeding the investigation into the alleged offending and is likely impeding additional complainants from coming forward and reporting similar experiences with the defendant".
The Crown said there was "significant public interest" in Paki's name being published.
Judge Crosbie said none of the matters raised by Paki reached the threshold of extreme hardship.

"There is a significant public interest in Mr Paki's name being published and the proceedings being open so that if there are other complainants ... they may feel as though they can safely come forward."
He said he was "not satisfied that publication of his name will result in any hardship beyond that which is an ordinary consequence of alleged offending like this".
"The threshold for "extreme hardship" is very high, and it has not been met in this case."
Paki then appealed to the High Court. Justice Rachel Dunningham declined the appeal in June, and Paki then went to the Court of Appeal.
On Thursday, the Court of Appeal rejected his application for leave to appeal.

Four years into a nationwide effort to make prison cells safer, almost 7000 known suicide risks remain in high-security and remand cells across the country.
Data released under the Official Information Act shows Corrections initially identified 2350 risks, before further inspections pushed the total to 13,335.
Corrections said it was committed to preventing self-harm and unnatural deaths and was prioritising cells based on risk as it continued the $6.79 million programme.
Just under half the risks - 6429 - had been removed or remediated to date.
The pace of progress has been criticised as deeply concerning by human rights monitors at Amnesty International and the mother of a prisoner who died in his cell in 2022.
Corrections said building constraints, high cell occupancy and other factors meant it would not be feasible to eliminate all of the risks, but said it was taking the programme seriously.

Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/crime-and-justice/2687617%2Fcorrections-still-tackling-almost-7000-prison-cell-risks

In findings released in August about the death of 30-year-old Nukuroa "Nuku" Strange in an Invercargill Prison cell in 2022, coroner Amelia Steel said it was unacceptable that Corrections had failed to act with urgency to mitigate a known risk .
Strange, who was on remand, had attempted suicide twice in the months before he died.
Although details of his death cannot be reported for legal reasons, the circumstances were the same as the death of another prisoner in the cell six years earlier.
Strange's mother, Kerry Ann Pink, said she remembered the moment during the inquest when she learnt about the previous death.
"It made me angry. I sort of had to hold on to my husband's leg and he had my fingernail imprint on his leg because I was just so angry. They could have prevented it but they didn't," she said.
Pink said she still regularly listened to an audio recording of her last phone call with her son and thought about all of the milestones he was missing.
Pink, who has organised suicide awareness events in Invercargill, said it should not take Corrections years to mitigate thousands of other known cell risks around the country.
"That is honestly piss poor. These are lives that they're playing with. It makes you angry. What happens if this is your child?" she said.
Corrections said staff were managing a growing number of people who had mental health and disability needs.
Deputy commissioner for men's prisons Neil Beales said Corrections was taking the programme seriously and staff were investing significant time, effort and attention to make cells safer.

"This isn't something we're doing on the side. It isn't something to do when we can. It's about not only looking at our existing infrastructure, particularly the older infrastructure where those risks were more prominent but embedding those lessons into how we build future infrastructure," he said.
Beales said the programme had grown in scope partly because officials had decided to take a more expansive view of cell risks rather than just removing the obvious hazards.
He said Corrections wanted to keep prisoners safe but also avoid making every cell "pretty much sterile".

"Where the department have done things for all of the best intentions - like putting televisions in cells or putting better toilet facilities - sometimes these things end up then presenting a risk that was not intended. We do want to try to make the living environments for people in prison as normal as we possibly can," he said.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/business/2687: Link: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2687493%2Ftonnes-of-asbestos-pulled-from-1b-queenstown-development-site
Thousands of tonnes of asbestos has been removed from the site of a more than $1 billion Queenstown development , according to newly-released council documents.
Lakeview is a residential, hospitality and retail precinct being built by Australian property developer 94 Feet as an extension of the town centre.
Queenstown Lakes District Council approved an extra $6.3 million to clear asbestos from the site in 2021, bringing the forecast site clearance cost to $12m.
Documents published by the council on Thursday suggest it was aware asbestos was present before demolition work began.

The initial plan was for excavation and off-site disposal of affected soil after environmental reporting confirmed asbestos fibres in the soil at four locations in 2020, with two above the relevant guidelines.
"As demolition and site-clearance progressed, considerably more asbestos was encountered than had been identified through the earlier investigations," the council said.
The final demolition report recorded 64.56 tonnes of asbestos-containing building material and 12,669 tonnes of asbestos-contaminated soil were removed over 12 months.
The council said the contractor reported the "significant" amount of contaminated soil was related to historic work at the site.

While the land under a development agreement had been remediated, other council-retained land including Lynch Block, the proposed hot pool site and Market Square might need further investigation and possible mitigation or remediation, the council said.
"On Lot 9, remediation work has been completed and measures are in place for the ongoing management of encapsulated asbestos-contaminated soil," the council said.

The wider infrastructure bill hit $74m in a January 2025 forecast, comprising $42m in subdivision costs, $14m for subdivision site clearance, $2m for ancillary site clearance and $16m for ancillary projects.
The extra work included additional transport and water infrastructure projects alongside the subdivision but with benefits for the wider network.
Of the forecast spending, $23 million was funded through rates and development contributions and $52m was reported as cost of sale, the council said.
The council said $48m had been invested in subdivision infrastructure in subsequent reports, with an additional $7m in deferred infrastructure.
The council planned to progressively sell "super lots" to the developer in stages, which would then develop them in line with an agreed plan for the entire precinct.
The council said the land deal provided for $75m in staged base land payments and it was also entitled to a share of the profit.
"This mechanism allows council to share in additional value realised over the life of the development," the council said.

In 2018, the council asked for pitches to develop the Lakeview Precinct, saying it wanted to maximise the financial return in way that minimised risk for ratepayers, create a thriving residential-focused mixed-used precinct and complete the project in eight to 10 years, subject to market conditions.
The council noted there should be a range of housing price points and types of homes, although affordable housing was not a requirement.
Housing insecurity, affordability and shortages have plagued Queenstown for years , with some people resorting to sharing rooms, hot-bedding, and living in garages, tents or cars.
About 300 people at a former Queenstown camping ground, many of whom were low-wage migrant workers, were evicted in 2019 to make way for the development

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/environment/2: Link: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/environment/2686586%2Freputational-damage-queenstown-council-warned-over-risks-from-wanaka-sludge-deal
Queenstown's mayor and two councillors were warned that a deal to spread Wānaka's sewage sludge on farmland in Central Otago would degrade the land and could pose a reputational risk for the council.

Details of the council's five-year agreement with contractor SJ Allen Holdings were revealed in documents released under the Local Government Official Information and Meetings Act and published by the council.
The documents show a council staff member told Mayor John Glover and councillors Gavin Bartlett and Cody Tucker that the contract would keep the council at "arm's length" from the risks.

Otago Regional Council granted non-notified resource consent in January allowing the district council to spread the sludge - a by-product of the wastewater treatment process - onto farmland near Lauder.
When Lauder locals discovered what was happening in September, there was an outcry over odour, dust, and potential effects on waterways.
Otago Regional Council has since been reviewing the consent, while Central Otago's mayor and councillors have written to their Queenstown counterparts asking them to reconsider the deal.
The documents show Glover, Bartlett and Tucker were first told about the potential arrangement in February, once SJ Allen had secured the regional council discharge consent.
The district council already had an arrangement with SJ Allen to truck Wānaka's sewage sludge to a landfill near Winton in Southland.

In the February letter, a staff member told Glover, Bartlett, and Tucker that the arrangement was becoming increasingly costly and that SJ Allen had come forward with an unsolicited alternative offer that could deliver a "magnitude of savings".

"SJ Allen approached us late last week advising that they had secured Resource Consent to dispose of wastewater sludge to land at a property located in Central Otago. They have offered to accept up to 2000 tonnes of material from our Wānaka WWTP [wastewater treatment plant] ...on the basis that we enter into a five-year commitment for this arrangement," the letter said.
The costs were redacted in the documents, but Glover previously told RNZ the arrangement saved the council about $1 million.
The staff member, whose name was redacted, said the district council would need to move quickly with a sunset clause in SJ Allen's conditional agreement to purchase the land at Lauder.
"Unfortunately, we are being put under some time pressure to advise SJ Allen of our interest in this offer," they said.
Otago Regional Council granted non-notified resource consent in January allowing the district council to spread the sludge onto farmland near Lauder.
The staff member told Glover, Bartlett, and Tucker that the deal came with "real and perceived" risks.
They said there was a notable difference between taking sewage sludge to landfill and spreading it on farmland.

"Wastewater sludges include contaminants and the land will be subject to degradation as a result of the application of these materials. The resource consent will have considered these within the assessment of environmental effects, and we will be at arm's length from this due to the contractual arrangement," they wrote.
"Risks associated with contamination and consent compliance will sit with the consent holder, but should issues occur, these could lead to reputational damage for QLDC."
Glover previously told RNZ his council had relied on the consent in good faith, but he was open to discussing alternative arrangements.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/voyager-1: NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft has become the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth. It passed the milestone on 18 November 2026.

A light-day is how far light travels in a whole day. Voyager 1 is now about 26 billion kilometres away, more than four times as far as Pluto is from the Sun. That means a signal sent from Earth takes 24 hours to reach the spacecraft.

Voyager 1 is about the size of a small car and launched from Florida, in the United States, on 5 September 1977. Along the way, it photographed Jupiter, Saturn and Titan, which is Saturn’s largest moon.

In 1990, it took 64 pictures that together made the first “family portrait” of the solar system. In 2012, it moved beyond the reach of the Sun’s magnetic field and into interstellar space, which is the space between stars.
The spacecraft has lasted far longer than anyone expected, but eight of its 10 science instruments no longer work. Within the next ten years, scientists may receive its very last signal.
For now, Voyager 1 is still sending back information about space beyond our solar system. Next year, it and its twin, Voyager 2, will both have been in space for 50 years.
Pānui: Kua tae a Voyager 1 ki te tawhiti o te light-day kotahi i Papatūānuku
Ko te waka ātea a NASA, a Voyager 1, te mea tuatahi i hangaia e te tangata kua tae ki te tawhiti o te light-day kotahi i Papatūānuku. I tae atu ia ki taua tohu i te 18 o Noema 2026.

Ko te light-day te tawhiti e haere ai te marama i te roanga o te rā katoa. Kei te tata ki te 26 piriona kiromita te tawhiti o Voyager 1 i tēnei wā, neke atu i te whā whakareatanga o te tawhiti o Pluto i te Rā. Nō reira, e 24 hāora te roa kia tae atu tētahi tohu i tukuna mai i Papatūānuku ki te waka ātea.

He rite te rahi o Voyager 1 ki tētahi motukā iti, ā, i whakarewaina mai i Florida, i Amerika, i te 5 o Hepetema 1977. I tōna haerenga, i tango whakaahua ia o Hupita, o Hatana, me Titan, te marama nui rawa o Hatana.

I te tau 1990, i tango ia i ngā whakaahua e 64, ā, i hanga ngātahi ai te “whakaahua whānau” tuatahi o te pūnaha o te Rā. I te tau 2012, i haere ia ki tua atu o te papa autō o te Rā, ki te ātea i waenganui i ngā whetū.

Kua roa ake te ora o te waka ātea i tā te katoa i whakaaro ai, engari kua kore e mahi ngā taputapu pūtaiao e waru o ōna taputapu e 10. I roto i ngā tau tekau e heke mai nei, tērā pea ka whiwhi ngā kaipūtaiao i tōna tohu whakamutunga rawa.
I tēnei wā, kei te tuku mai tonu a Voyager 1 i ngā mōhiohio mō te ātea i tua atu o tō tātou pūnaha o te Rā. Ā tērā tau, ka 50 tau a ia me tōna māhanga, a Voyager 2, e noho ana i te ātea.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/leaders-o: US President Donald Trump, China’s President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin are holding their first-ever three-way meeting. The talks are taking place on 19 November 2026 in Shenzhen, China.
The meeting is happening alongside Apec, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. Apec is a big gathering of countries in the region that meet to talk about trade.
No one knows exactly what the leaders will discuss in private, but there are some big issues affecting all three countries.
The war between the US and Israel on one side and Iran on the other has hurt economies around the world. China is the biggest buyer of Iran’s oil.
The US and China are also racing to become the world leader in artificial intelligence, or AI.

Russia has been more cut off from other countries since it invaded Ukraine in 2022. Experts think a breakthrough on ending that war is unlikely. European leaders, and especially Ukraine, are worried about talks that don’t include anyone from Ukraine.

Vladimir Putin has led Russia since 1999, sometimes as President and sometimes as Prime Minister. Donald Trump began his second term as US President in 2025, after first serving from 2017 to 2021. Xi Jinping has been China’s leader since 2012.
BBC China Correspondent Laura Bicker said the meeting is a chance for President Xi to show China as a bridge between big countries.
Details of what the three leaders agree on, if anything, are expected once the talks are over.
Pānui: Ka hui ngā kaiārahi o Amerika, Haina me Rūhia mō te wā tuatahi

Kei te hui tahi te Perehitini o Amerika, a Donald Trump, te Perehitini o Haina, a Xi Jinping, me te Perehitini o Rūhia, a Vladimir Putin, mō te wā tuatahi rawa. Kei te tū te hui i te 19 o Noema 2026 ki Shenzhen, i Haina.
Kei te tū te hui i te taha o Apec, arā, te Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. He hui nui a Apec mā ngā whenua o tēnei rohe hei kōrero mō te hokohoko.
Kāore tētahi e mōhio pū ki ngā kōrero a ngā kaiārahi i tā rātou hui tūmataiti, engari he take nui kei te pā ki ngā whenua e toru.
Kua raru ngā ōhanga huri noa i te ao i te pakanga i waenganui i Amerika me Iharaira i tētahi taha, me Iran i tērā taha. Ko Haina te kaihoko nui rawa o te hinu o Iran.
Kei te whakataetae hoki a Amerika rāua ko Haina kia noho ko rātou te kaiārahi o te ao mō te atamai hangahanga, arā, te AI.

Kua noho mokemoke ake a Rūhia i ētahi atu whenua mai i tana whakaeke i Ūkareina i te tau 2022. E whakaaro ana ngā tohunga kāore pea e kitea he huarahi hou hei whakamutu i taua pakanga. Kei te māharahara ngā kaiārahi o Ūropi, otirā a Ūkareina, mō ngā hui kāore he tangata nō Ūkareina e uru ana.

Kua ārahi a Vladimir Putin i a Rūhia mai i te tau 1999, i ētahi wā hei Perehitini, i ētahi wā hei Pirimia. I tīmata a Donald Trump i tana wāhanga tuarua hei Perehitini o Amerika i te tau 2025, i muri i tana wāhanga tuatahi mai i te tau 2017 ki te tau 2021. Ko Xi Jinping te kaiārahi o Haina mai i te tau 2012.
E ai ki te kaikawe kōrero o te BBC i Haina, a Laura Bicker, he whai wāhitanga tēnei hui mā te Perehitini Xi ki te whakaatu i a Haina hei arawhiti i waenganui i ngā whenua nunui.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/study-fin: If your cat keeps meowing at you, it might be asking for a hand. A new study from the University of São Paulo in Brazil has found that cats use meows, along with eye contact, to ask their owners for help.

The researchers visited 38 cats in their own homes. Each cat was given a treat trapped inside a small plastic box with holes in it, so it could see and smell the snack but couldn’t get it out by itself.

When a person was in the room, the cats meowed 85 times, compared with just 20 times when they were alone. That’s about four times as many. Overall, the cats were 16 times more likely to meow when a human was around.

With no person nearby, the cats mostly stayed quiet, stood still and stared at the door. When a person was there, the cats meowed while looking straight at them, and kept glancing back and forth between the human and the box.
The researchers also found that feral cats meow much less than pet cats. Feral cats live on their own and don’t belong to anyone.
The study was published in the journal Animal Behaviour . It says meowing isn’t just a cat showing how it feels. It plays a “communicative role”, which means it’s a way for cats to talk to people.
So next time your cat meows and stares at you, it may simply be asking for a little help.

Mēnā ka miau tonu tō ngeru ki a koe, tērā pea kei te tono āwhina ia. Kua kitea e tētahi rangahau hou nā te University of São Paulo i Parīhi, ka miau ngā ngeru, ka titiro hoki ki ngā kanohi, hei tono āwhina i ō rātou rangatira.

I toro atu ngā kairangahau ki ngā ngeru e 38 i ō rātou ake kāinga. I hoatu he kai reka ki ia ngeru, kua mau i roto i tētahi pouaka kirihou iti he kōputaputa ōna. Ka kite, ka hongi te ngeru i te kai, engari kāore e taea e ia anake te tango mai.

I te wā he tangata i roto i te rūma, e 85 ngā miau a ngā ngeru, engari e 20 noa iho i te wā i a rātou anake. Tata ki te whā whakareatanga te nui ake. Ina whakarāpopotohia, e 16 whakareatanga te nui ake o te tūponotanga ka miau ngā ngeru mēnā he tangata kei reira.

Ki te kore he tangata i te taha, i noho wahangū te nuinga o ngā ngeru, i tū mārie, ā, i titiro atu ki te kūaha. I te wā he tangata kei reira, i miau ngā ngeru me te titiro tika atu ki taua tangata, ā, i huri haere tō rātou titiro i waenganui i te tangata me te pouaka.
I kitea anō e ngā kairangahau he iti ake te miau a ngā ngeru mohoao i tō ngā ngeru mōkai. Ka noho motuhake ngā ngeru mohoao, ehara i te mōkai a tētahi.

I tāngia te rangahau ki te hautaka Animal Behaviour . E ai ki te rangahau, ehara te miau i te whakaatu noa a te ngeru i ōna kare-ā-roto. He “tūranga whakawhitiwhiti kōrero” tōna, arā, he huarahi mā ngā ngeru hei kōrero ki te tangata.
Nō reira, ā muri ake nei, ina miau tō ngeru me te titiro mai ki a koe, tērā pea kei te tono āwhina noa iho ia.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/bee-swarm: Auckland is seeing about twice as many bee swarms as usual this spring, with local beekeepers getting up to 10 calls for help a day.
Ken Brown, president of the Auckland Beekeepers Club, said the milder winter was the reason. He said the swarms had started about four weeks earlier than normal.
A swarm happens when a hive gets too crowded. The bees raise a new queen, and the old queen flies off with up to half the colony to start a new home somewhere else.
Brown said this is natural and “a sign of a good, strong, healthy hive”. In one backyard, thousands of bees turned up at once.

Phil Lester, a biology professor at Victoria University, said bees had been breeding well and growing their numbers. He said bees are important because they pollinate many of the crops we grow for food.
Swarms are being spotted all over New Zealand, and experts think swarming season could last until January.
Brown said swarms are not much of a risk to people, even if they can be a surprise to see in the city.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/darth-vad: A lightsaber used by Darth Vader in two Star Wars films has sold for US$4.875 million, making it the most expensive Star Wars item ever sold at auction.
The lightsaber was used in The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi. It appeared in the famous duel in Cloud City, where Darth Vader tells Luke Skywalker, “I am your father.”
It was sold by Heritage Auctions in the United States, at an event called the Ultimate Star Wars Auction. In an auction, people bid against each other, and whoever offers the most money wins.
The sale beat the old record, set in July, when Luke Skywalker’s lightsaber sold for US$3.75 million. That means Vader’s lightsaber went for more than US$1 million extra.
The auction also included 27 other lightsabers, along with items from all nine main Star Wars films and other movies and TV shows.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/des-bucki: New Zealand Football has confirmed Des Buckingham as the new head coach of the All Whites, New Zealand’s men’s football team, starting on 1 July 2027 and continuing through to the 2030 FIFA World Cup.
Buckingham will also lead the New Zealand Men’s Under-23 team as they aim to qualify for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games.

He is not new to New Zealand football. Buckingham lived and worked here for seven years, including as an assistant coach with the All Whites and head coach of the Men’s Under-23 side. In 2019, he guided that team to qualification for the Tokyo 2020 Olympics and to New Zealand’s first-ever Pacific Games football gold medal.
That same year, he led the Men’s Under-20 team to the country’s highest-ever finish at a men’s FIFA World Cup tournament, including a record 5-0 win over Honduras.

Since then, Buckingham has coached around the world, most recently as head coach of Al-Kholood in Saudi Arabia. He also led English club Oxford United into the Championship division for the first time in 25 years.
New Zealand Football chief executive Andrew Pragnell said the appointment was a big moment for the sport.
“I’m incredibly proud to announce Des as the new All Whites Coach,” Pragnell said. “This is huge for New Zealand Football and the future success of both NZF and the All Whites.”
Fans will have to wait until next July to see Buckingham take charge.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/new-parki: From December, visitors will have to pay to park at some of New Zealand’s most popular outdoor spots, as the Department of Conservation (DOC) rolls out paid parking more widely.
Sites getting paid car parks include Goat Island north of Auckland, the Tasman Glacier, Kura Tāwhiti/Castle Hill, the Routeburn Divide, and the Kepler Track control gates, among others.

At most of these places, the cost will be $2.50 for every half hour, or $20 for the whole day. At Goat Island, the first 10 minutes are free for quick drop-offs and pick-ups, and there is a separate $15 daily rate over winter.

People who live nearby can buy a $10 annual permit instead, which covers unlimited parking all year for up to two vehicles. School groups, DOC volunteers and community groups will be able to apply for an exemption.
The new fees follow a trial that started in the South Island earlier this year, at places like Punakaiki’s Pancake Rocks, Franz Josef and Aoraki Mount Cook.
David Butt, DOC’s director of heritage and visitors, said the money raised, expected to be about $3 million over the next year, would help look after the sites.
“We will use paid parking to generate revenue to contribute to the long-term care of places like Goat Island,” he said.

Cameras will keep track of cars coming in and out, and anyone who doesn’t pay could be issued a $75 breach notice – so if your family is planning a summer trip to one of these spots, it might pay to bring some extra coins.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/robert-pa: British actor Robert Pattinson has been announced as the next James Bond, becoming the seventh actor to play the famous spy in the 64-year-old film series.
Amazon MGM Studios shared the news with a short video clip showing Pattinson, 40, stepping out of the shadows holding a gun, the character’s classic pose.
Pattinson is well known for playing Edward Cullen in the Twilight films, Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter, and the title role in The Batman. He is currently filming the sequel, The Batman Part II.
“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement.

The new film, known for now simply as “Bond 26,” will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, who also directed the Dune films. “I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond,” Villeneuve said.

Filming is expected to begin next year. It will be the first Bond film made since Amazon bought the MGM film studio in 2022, and the first where the Broccoli family, who have led the franchise for decades, haven’t personally chosen the lead actor.

The Bond films, based on novels by Ian Fleming, have earned more than US$7 billion at the box office since the first film in 1962. Fans will have to wait a while yet to see Pattinson in action as 007.
